title: Camp 4 close
hook: the whole strand, all 21 Camp 1 words, the Gita done
tomorrow: Isha Upanishad (18 verses, one week): "all this is pervaded by the Lord" (1 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, anasakti: the Gita in the world. Thoreau at the pond, Tilak in a cell, Vivekananda, Gandhi. Your line was who else carried it. Today, the last day of the camp.

In ancient India, a student lived for years in the teacher's house, learning the Vedas by heart. When the studies were done, there was a ceremony called samavartana: the return home. The student bathed, put on new clothes, and the teacher gave a last talk. One version of that talk survives in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Speak the truth. Practice dharma. Don't neglect your study. Treat your mother, your father, your teacher and your guest as the divine. Then the student walked home, carrying it all. Today is your samavartana.
screen: `YEARS IN THE TEACHER'S HOUSE.` → `SPEAK THE TRUTH. PRACTICE DHARMA.` → `THEN, THE WALK HOME.`

segments.voice: Look at what you're carrying. It started with twenty-one words, back in camp one. Namaste. Om. Dharma. Shanti. Pranam. Ganesha. Mantra. Puja. Karma. Atman. Brahman. Guru. Japa. Arti. Seva. Bhakti. Ahimsa. Maya. Moksha. Satsang. And the twenty-first, the Gita itself, the mountain ahead, with its line: you have the right to act, not to the fruit. Then the stories, then the practices. Then, for seventy-five days, the text itself, a few verses at a time. Chapter one, a man collapsing in a chariot. Chapter eighteen, the same man standing up: my confusion is gone. This last week drew it together. The last instruction: do not grieve. Sanjaya's closing: wherever Krishna and Arjuna are, there is victory. The whole book in one session. Your twelve verses, chosen by you. One verse a day, going forward. And the people who carried it before you. Here's what's worth saying plainly. Plenty of people keep a Gita on the shelf and never read it through. You have. Not in a weekend, not by skimming, but slowly, one piece of the conversation at a time. That counts. Tomorrow the path goes deeper. Camp five is the depths: the Upanishads, the texts the Gita itself draws on. First comes the Isha Upanishad, eighteen verses in a week, and its first line: all this is pervaded by the Lord. But today, just take the bath, put on the new clothes, and walk home carrying it.
screen: `TWENTY-ONE WORDS.` · `SEVENTY-FIVE DAYS OF THE TEXT.` · `YOU READ IT THROUGH.` · `NEXT: THE DEPTHS.` · then, large: `GRADUATION.`

segments.voice: Let the camp one words pass through you once more, slowly, one breath each if you like, in any order: namaste, om, dharma, shanti. Then let the Gita come as a single picture, the chariot, the two, the dawn over the field, and bring to mind your one verse for today. Hold it; you don't have to do anything with it, just notice that it's yours now.
Graduation. In the old tradition, samavartana, the student's return home, with a last teaching: speak the truth, practice dharma, don't neglect your study.
Your line: you actually read it, slowly, one piece at a time. Tomorrow, the depths. Camp four, complete.

howItsDone: In traditional Hindu education, the end of study was marked by samavartana, the student's ceremonial return home, and the teacher's final advice in Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 is still recited at some convocations in India; many Hindus mark finishing the Gita with a full recitation or a small puja.

original.note: Sanskrit: samavartana, returning home: the rite marking the end of a student's years of Vedic study.

what a scholar hears: samavartana is one of the Hindu samskaras; Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11 ('satyam vada, dharmam chara, svadhyayan ma pramadah') is traditionally read as the teacher's convocation address.

chat.says: What's the big deal about finishing the Gita, anyway?
options: Lots of people own one and never read it. Reading it slowly really counts.
It means you've mastered Hinduism and can stop studying now.
Nothing much; it was only a warm-up and doesn't count for much.
